source: Poirier, Nairne, Morin, Zimmermann, Koutmeridou & Fowler (2012) Memory as discrimination: a challenge to the encoding-retrieval match principle (JEP:LMC 38:16-29)
finding: Four cued-recognition experiments crossed encoding-retrieval match with cue diagnostic value. Adding a shared (non-unique) cue to a unique cue raised match but slowed retrieval.
numbers: Exp1 (N=25): RT effect of cue type F(2,46)=5.53 p<.01; one-unique+one-shared slower than one-unique t(24)=2.77 and than two-unique t(24)=2.46; accuracy above 90% in all conditions. Slowing about 200-300 ms across experiments.
quote: increasing the encoding-retrieval match can hinder performance if the increase simultaneously reduces how specifically cues predict a target
limits: Learning trained to high accuracy, so the effect is on speed not accuracy; small sets of 3-4 targets; one-tailed planned tests.
agent_relevance: A matching extra cue that also points to other candidates costs time. Prefer one unique key over a bigger overlapping key.

source: Poirier, Nairne, Morin, Zimmermann, Koutmeridou & Fowler (2012) Memory as discrimination: a challenge to the encoding-retrieval match principle (JEP:LMC 38:16-29)
finding: Exp2 repeated the pattern with familiar words as cues and targets.
numbers: N=23. Cue-type RT F(2,44)=5.18 p<.01; one-unique+one-shared slower than one-unique t(22)=2.54 and than two-unique t(22)=2.62. Accuracy effect F(2,44)=3.35 p<.05, two-unique slightly better than one-unique t(22)=2.85.
limits: Same lab, same paradigm, different stimuli.
agent_relevance: The effect does not depend on novel stimuli.

source: Poirier, Nairne, Morin, Zimmermann, Koutmeridou & Fowler (2012) Memory as discrimination: a challenge to the encoding-retrieval match principle (JEP:LMC 38:16-29)
finding: Exp4 (animal drawings as targets, 75% criterion, easier task) still found slowing for a complete but non-discriminative cue set.
numbers: N=21. RT effect F(2,40)=10.58 p<.001; one-unique+one-shared slower than one-unique t(20)=2.89 p=.005 and than two-unique t(20)=4.73 p<.001. Training brought accuracy above 98%. One-unique vs two-unique not reliable.
limits: Same lab; difference between one-unique and two-unique not reliable.
agent_relevance: The slowing is not a weak-cue artefact: the shared cue was fully learned.

source: Poirier, Nairne, Morin, Zimmermann, Koutmeridou & Fowler (2012) Memory as discrimination: a challenge to the encoding-retrieval match principle (JEP:LMC 38:16-29)
finding: Control for left-to-right reading: shared cue on the left vs unique cue on the left gave no reliable RT difference in any experiment.
numbers: Median RT comparison of cue position in the one-unique+one-shared condition, run in Exp1, 2, 3 and 4; none reliable.
limits: Within-lab control; no pre-registration.
agent_relevance: Rules out a simple serial-processing explanation of the discrimination cost.

source: Poirier, Nairne, Morin, Zimmermann, Koutmeridou & Fowler (2012) Memory as discrimination: a challenge to the encoding-retrieval match principle (JEP:LMC 38:16-29)
finding: Memory-as-discrimination uses a choice rule: P(recall target | cue) = similarity(cue,target) / sum of similarity(cue, every candidate). Match raises the numerator, competitors raise the denominator, so more match can mean better, same or worse.
numbers: Rule from Nairne 2001/2002 and Nosofsky 1986; Poirier et al. test the 'worse' prediction.
limits: A ratio choice rule is not a mechanism; Badham et al. note it only works if the cue-target binding was formed.
agent_relevance: Score a memory key by target similarity divided by similarity to all other stored items, not by overlap alone.

source: Poirier, Nairne, Morin, Zimmermann, Koutmeridou & Fowler (2012) Memory as discrimination: a challenge to the encoding-retrieval match principle (JEP:LMC 38:16-29)
finding: The authors separate encoding specificity (a cue must have been encoded with the item) from the popular 'more match helps' reading. Cue overload (Craik & Tulving: one, four or eight targets per cue) lowers recall as targets per cue grow.
numbers: Craik & Tulving result as reported second-hand: retrieval success inversely proportional to number of targets per cue.
quote: no cue, however strongly associated with the TBR item or otherwise related to it, can be effective unless the TBR item is specifically encoded with respect to that cue (Thomson & Tulving 1970, quoted)
limits: Second-hand description of earlier studies.
agent_relevance: The original principle is narrower than the popular reading. Do not build the scaffold on 'more overlap is better'.

source: Goh & Lu (2012) Testing the myth of the encoding-retrieval match (Mem Cogn 40:28-39)
finding: Exp1 (N=40, cue-target pairs, category name as second cue): extra match helped when overload was low but not when overload was high.
numbers: Low overload: high-match M=.37 vs low-match .24, F(1,39)=17.14 p<.001. High overload: .28 vs .28, F<1. Interaction F(1,39)=13.89 p<.01.
limits: Cued recall of unrelated words; second cue was the category name.
agent_relevance: Independent support for Nairne: the match gain vanishes when the extra cue also fits many competitors.

source: Goh & Lu (2012) Testing the myth of the encoding-retrieval match (Mem Cogn 40:28-39)
finding: Exp2 (N=43) made the overload less obvious (3 same-category foils instead of 9). Same pattern.
numbers: Low overload: high-match M=.31 vs low-match .20, F(1,41)=12.15 p<.01. High overload .24 vs .23, F<1. Interaction F(1,41)=5.23 p<.05.
limits: Manipulation check: most participants did not notice same-category targets, so a strategy artefact is unlikely.
agent_relevance: The result holds even when people do not exploit the overload structure.

source: Goh & Lu (2012) Testing the myth of the encoding-retrieval match (Mem Cogn 40:28-39)
finding: Exp3 (N=40) used the Thomson & Tulving (1970) design with overload held constant. Studied weak cues still beat strong extralist cues at both overload levels, so match still helps when overload is equated.
numbers: Cue type F(2,78)=38.33 p<.001: intralist M=.32, strong extralist .25, weak extralist .09. Overload F(1,39)=90.24: low .31 vs high .14. Cue x overload F<1.
limits: Authors note they showed only two of Nairne's three outcomes (better, no change), not 'worse'. So 'match is a myth' is too strong when overload is held constant.
agent_relevance: Match and distinctiveness both matter. Match is the numerator; distinct keys stop it being cancelled.

source: Goh & Lu (2012) Testing the myth of the encoding-retrieval match (Mem Cogn 40:28-39)
finding: Conclusion: the diagnostic value of the cue predicts recall better than absolute match, but they do not say match is irrelevant.
quote: the diagnostic value of the cue is the important factor in predicting cue efficacy, rather than the absolute value of the encoding-retrieval match
limits: Wording taken from the discussion text as extracted.
agent_relevance: A balanced position for the schema: use both a matching and a discriminating key.

source: Higham (2002) Strong cues are not necessarily weak: Thomson and Tulving (1970) and the encoding specificity principle revisited (Mem Cogn 30:67-80)
finding: Re-ran Thomson & Tulving (1970) with a two-stage test separating retrieval, monitoring and report bias. The classic finding that strong extralist cues do not beat no cue is a report-bias effect.
numbers: Free report: weak-cue retrieval .26, strong-cue .07, no-cue .08. Forced report: strong-cue .26, weak-cue .28. Cue type x report type F(1,30)=97.22 p<.001. Weak-cue free .24 and .29 vs no-cue .08.
quote: their cue-reinstatement manipulation affected free-report retrieval, but once report bias and monitoring effects were removed by forcing output, retrieval was unaffected
limits: One paradigm; point system for withholding; forced responses may include guesses.
agent_relevance: The best-known demonstration of encoding specificity is largely about whether people dare to answer. Confidence gating in an agent can hide good keys.

source: Higham (2002) Strong cues are not necessarily weak: Thomson and Tulving (1970) and the encoding specificity principle revisited (Mem Cogn 30:67-80)
finding: Monitoring was poorer with strong extralist cues, so people withheld correct answers and used a more conservative criterion for them.
numbers: Strong-cue condition had worse monitoring and more conservative bias than weak-cue; trial vs phase collection of blanks had no effect (largest F(1,30)=1.27).
limits: Monitoring and bias values read from text only, not all cells extracted.
agent_relevance: Separate 'retrieval found it' from 'the agent trusted it'. Check withheld candidates before declaring a miss.

source: Postman (1975) Tests of the generality of the principle of encoding specificity (Mem Cogn 3:663-672)
finding: Exp1 varied the strength of input and output cues. Strong output cues beat weak ones regardless of the input cue. A same-cue advantage existed but did not make strong extralist cues useless.
numbers: Stringent scores (6 items per cell): new-cue-at-test (N-C) subset: W-S 3.17 vs W-W .17; same-cue (C-C): S-S 4.29, W-S 3.04, W-W 2.33. Output cue strength F(1,92)=94.68.
limits: Mixed lists with half the items uncued to weaken the pairwise-associative set. Postman says earlier failures of strong extralist cues came from that set.
agent_relevance: Strong, naturally related cues work if the task does not tell people to expect only the original pair. Task framing changes which keys work.

source: Postman (1975) Tests of the generality of the principle of encoding specificity (Mem Cogn 3:663-672)
finding: With strong cues, recall was almost equal for same-cue and new-cue items, which strains an encoding-specificity reading.
numbers: Condition S-S: C-C 4.29 vs N-C 4.00; W-S: C-C 3.04 vs N-C 3.17 (stringent scores).
quote: It is the virtual equality of scores for the C-C and N-C subsets in the presence of strong cues that creates difficulties for a specificity interpretation
limits: Author reads this through generation-recognition models; weak-cue conditions did show a same-cue advantage (W-W 2.33 vs .17).
agent_relevance: Cue similarity to the target from prior knowledge can stand in for having been encoded together.

source: Postman (1975) Tests of the generality of the principle of encoding specificity (Mem Cogn 3:663-672)
finding: Exp2 on recognition failure of recallable words: with independent groups and no intrasession transfer, recall was not found superior to recognition.
numbers: Design: two generation groups (high and mixed associates, 2 generated items each) plus recognition and recall controls; strong extralist cues p=.52 vs weak input cues. Only the abstract-level conclusion was extracted; per-group numbers not read.
quote: The phenomena of cue-dependent forgetting that have been interpreted as evidence for the principle of encoding specificity appear to have limited generality
limits: No per-cell numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Recognition-failure effects depend on test details. Do not treat them as a law.

source: Stein (1977) The effects of cue-target uniqueness on cued recall performance (Mem Cogn 5:319-322)
finding: Encoding instruction manipulated how unique each cue-target pair was. Simile rating (unique relation) gave far better cued recall than a hardness rating (shared relation) on the same list.
numbers: Exp1 N=40: mean correct 14.31 (simile) vs 5.24 (hard-soft) of 24, t(38)=8.9 p<.001. Given a yes rating: 78% vs 36%, t(38)=5.93. Intrusions .5 vs 1.9, t(38)=2.98.
limits: Between-subjects, undergraduates, 24 pairs; text partly garbled by OCR.
agent_relevance: Early direct case that pair-level uniqueness, not mere co-presence, sets cue power. Write distinctive links when storing.

source: Stein (1977) The effects of cue-target uniqueness on cued recall performance (Mem Cogn 5:319-322)
finding: Pair recognition was also better under unique (simile) encoding, but single-word recognition was not.
numbers: Exp2 pair recognition: 11.2 vs 9.3 of 12 correct, false positives .40 vs 1.7, t(38)=4.61 p<.001. Exp3 single-item recognition: 42.0 vs 43.3 of 48, t(38)=1.56 n.s.
limits: Item recognition is insensitive to relational uniqueness.
agent_relevance: Distinct relation encoding helps association retrieval, not item familiarity.

source: Smith & Vela (2001) Environmental context-dependent memory: a review and meta-analysis (Psychon Bull Rev 8:203-220)
finding: Meta-analysis of incidental environmental context-dependent memory: a modest but reliable effect. Context reinstatement is the classic match manipulation.
numbers: d=.28 (95% CI +/-.05) across 93 effect sizes; reinstatement d=.23 (n=66), interference reduction d=.68 (n=10), multiple context d=.45 (n=7); heterogeneity QT=193.22 p<.001. 18 of 93 effects above d=.80.
limits: Heterogeneous effects, many small studies.
agent_relevance: Environmental match gives a small average benefit. Do not over-invest in recreating context.

source: Smith & Vela (2001) Environmental context-dependent memory: a review and meta-analysis (Psychon Bull Rev 8:203-220)
finding: Outshining test: when people process noncontextual (associative) information at input, the room-change effect shrinks. Support was mixed.
numbers: Associative processing at input d=.13 (+/-.10, n=29); nonassociative d=.33 (n=12); unsure d=.38 (n=42); associative vs nonassociative chi2=6.67 p<.01. Test type (free recall d=.29, recognition d=.27, cued recall d=.25 n=3) not significant, QB=.21.
quote: context dependent memory effects are less likely to occur under conditions in which the immediate environment is likely to be suppressed
limits: The test-type moderator predicted by outshining did not appear; authors note recall-recognition comparisons used highly associable word lists.
agent_relevance: Context helps mostly when richer cues are missing. If the agent has strong meaning keys, extra environment tags add little.

source: Smith & Vela (2001) Environmental context-dependent memory: a review and meta-analysis (Psychon Bull Rev 8:203-220)
finding: Moderators: switching experimenter and a longer retention interval increased the context effect.
numbers: Longest delay (1 day to 1 week) gave a significantly larger effect than shorter delays; mental reinstatement studies n=10.
limits: Study-level covariates; correlational.
agent_relevance: Context cues matter more late, when other cues have faded.

source: Smith & Vela (2001) Environmental context-dependent memory: a review and meta-analysis (Psychon Bull Rev 8:203-220)
finding: The meta-analysis reconciles Fernandez & Glenberg (1985), titled 'Changing environmental context does not reliably affect memory': with associative processing at input, effects were rarely above zero.
numbers: In 28 studies with associative processing at input, effect sizes were rarely greater than zero; 7 of the 8 Fernandez and Glenberg cases used associative processing.
limits: Interpretation by Smith and Vela.
agent_relevance: A failed-replication pattern explained by a moderator: strong item-level processing swamps context.

source: Badham, Poirier, Gandhi, Hadjivassiliou & Maylor (2016) Aging and memory as discrimination: influences of encoding specificity, cue overload and prior knowledge
finding: Young and older adults learned cue-cue-target triplets (schema-consistent or not) in Exp1. Memory-as-discrimination held in both age groups: the shared cue slowed retrieval.
numbers: Cuing condition F(2,114)=55.94 p<.001, partial eta2=.50; one-unique faster than one-unique+one-shared F(1,57)=10.30; age x cuing condition F(2,114)=4.83 p=.010.
quote: cues increasing encoding-retrieval match did not benefit memory unless they also improved discrimination between the target and competitors
limits: N about 60 after training (df 57); repeats Poirier Exp4 paradigm with extra learning phase.
agent_relevance: Discrimination cost is age-invariant, so it looks like a general mechanism.

source: Badham, Poirier, Gandhi, Hadjivassiliou & Maylor (2016) Aging and memory as discrimination: influences of encoding specificity, cue overload and prior knowledge
finding: Exp2 cued recall without training: higher match helped only when the reinstated background image was unique, not when shared, and it helped older adults more.
numbers: Match F(1,59)=16.09 p<.001, partial eta2=.21; match x encoding condition F(1,59)=10.95 p=.002 (unique t(60)=4.35, shared t<1); age x match F(1,59)=6.66 p=.012: older t(30)=3.73 p<.001, young t(29)=1.60 p=.120. Cue overload F(1,59)=10.68 p=.002.
limits: Large age gap in recall (F(1,59)=80.99); N about 61.
agent_relevance: Match helps when the extra cue is unique, and weaker memories gain more from richer matching cues.

source: Badham, Poirier, Gandhi, Hadjivassiliou & Maylor (2016) Aging and memory as discrimination: influences of encoding specificity, cue overload and prior knowledge
finding: Prior knowledge (schemas) mattered: schema-consistent groupings were learned and retrieved faster, and reduced age gaps.
numbers: Training age effect F(1,70)=38.54 p<.001, partial eta2=.36; retrieval age deficit F(1,57)=112.13, partial eta2=.66; schema consistency F(1,57)=35.79, partial eta2=.39.
limits: Picture sets built from category exemplars only.
agent_relevance: Prior structure is another route to cue distinctiveness. Links to the schemas subfield.

source: Badham, Poirier, Gandhi, Hadjivassiliou & Maylor (2016) Aging and memory as discrimination: influences of encoding specificity, cue overload and prior knowledge
finding: The authors say Goh and Lu (2012) left the overloaded cue unstudied and relied on existing links, which may have weakened that manipulation.
limits: An interpretive claim in the paper, not a measurement.
agent_relevance: Tests of the match critique need competitor links that were actually trained.

source: Dinh, Ding, Qu & Thilakarathna (2026) Memory retrieval in transformers: insights from the encoding specificity principle
finding: Transformer attention is mapped to cue-based retrieval: queries are the retrieval context, keys index traces, values hold content. Swapping keys, values or both between factual and counterfactual prompts tested this.
numbers: Seven open models (Llama 2-7b and 13b, Llama 3.1-8b, Olmo 2-13b, Qwen 2.5-14b, Phi-4, GPT-NeoX-20b). Swapping V gives counterfactual answers (50% in Olmo 2 to 90% in Qwen 2.5). Swapping K and V: 100% hallucination in all models. Swapping K only: factual accuracy about 30-40%.
quote: with V intact, the memory content must be available but models forget due to retrieval failure
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed; counterfactual accuracy lowest in GPT-NeoX and OLMo-2; interventions, not natural use.
agent_relevance: Keys decide what gets retrieved. A mis-keyed item is 'forgotten' though stored. Key quality is the lever.

source: Dinh, Ding, Qu & Thilakarathna (2026) Memory retrieval in transformers: insights from the encoding specificity principle
finding: Keywords-as-cues: specific attention neurons carry context-defining keywords; perturbing them lowers verbatim recall of memorised books.
numbers: Books tested with ROUGE-L recall and BERTScore; LXT keywords gave the largest memorisation drop but MAUVE and repetition degraded markedly; GPT-4o keywords and their method were milder.
quote: These keywords can be extracted from identified neurons and further contribute to downstream applications such as unlearning
limits: Applies to memorised pretraining text, not in-context retrieval; Llama 2 anomaly attributed by authors to its 32k vocabulary.
agent_relevance: Distinctive keywords are the retrieval handle even inside the model. Supports keyword-centred keys.

source: Guo, Wu & Yiu (2026) The interference gap: comparing retrieval bounds in human memory and RAG systems
finding: Fan effect (cue overload) in humans vs retrievers: accuracy falls with more associations per cue. Humans are less sensitive than dense retrieval.
limits: Preprint; the authors say data cannot separate encoding specificity, temporal binding and gating; only human-DPR slope CIs do not overlap.
agent_relevance: A cue shared by many items hurts a dense retriever more than a person. Make keys unique per memory.

source: Guo, Wu & Yiu (2026) The interference gap: comparing retrieval bounds in human memory and RAG systems
finding: Serial position: humans show recency, DPR primacy, HippoRAG balanced. Encoding specificity is named as one candidate for the lower human interference slope.
numbers: DPR positions 1/10/20: 89.2/61.4/68.3%; HippoRAG 86.4/68.9/78.1%. System x position F(4,536)=8.73 p<.001, partial eta2=.061.
limits: Authors state mechanism attribution is 'a research programme rather than a finding'.
agent_relevance: Retrieval systems show human-like interference but worse; distinctive context features are a design option.

source: Cuconasu et al. (2024) The power of noise: redefining retrieval for RAG systems
finding: In RAG prompts, related-but-wrong (distracting) passages hurt accuracy. Cue-similar competitors lower accuracy, an LLM analogue of cue overload.
numbers: Gold-only baseline vs one distractor: drop up to 0.24 (-25%); more distractors cut accuracy by over 0.38 (-67%) in some cases; Llama2 with 18 distractors 0.37, 0.23, 0.17 by gold position.
quote: adding just one distracting document causes a sharp reduction in accuracy
limits: Natural-Questions-style benchmark on Llama2-7b, MPT, Phi-2, Falcon; closed-book 0.11, 0.12, 0.05, 0.11.
agent_relevance: Similar but non-answering items are costly. Prune near-duplicates at retrieval.

source: Cuconasu et al. (2024) The power of noise: redefining retrieval for RAG systems
finding: Random unrelated documents placed near the query raised accuracy, an unexplained effect.
numbers: Up to +35% accuracy with random documents added; changes significant vs gold-only by Wilcoxon p<.01 except marked cells.
quote: adding random documents in the prompt improves the LLM accuracy by up to 35%
limits: Mechanism unknown; authors call it counter-intuitive; position-dependent.
agent_relevance: Do not read this as 'add noise'; it shows retrieval behaviour is not simple match.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Lost in the middle: how language models use long contexts
finding: Position of the relevant item changes use of context: best at start or end, worse in the middle. With 20 or 30 documents performance fell below closed-book.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo can drop by more than 20% when the answer is in the middle; closed-book 56.1%; with 20 and 30 documents multi-document QA is below closed-book.
quote: performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context
limits: 2023 models (GPT-3.5, Claude-1.3, MPT, LongChat); newer models may differ.
agent_relevance: Position is another cue; where a retrieved item sits is part of its distinctiveness.

source: Anthropic (2024) Introducing Contextual Retrieval (blog)
finding: Contextual Retrieval prepends a 50-100 token description of where a chunk sits in its document before embedding and BM25. This adds distinguishing context to the key.
numbers: Top-20 retrieval failure: baseline 5.7%, contextual embeddings 3.7% (-35%), plus contextual BM25 2.9% (-49%), plus reranking 1.9% (-67%).
limits: Vendor blog, internal datasets, not peer reviewed; effect depends on corpus.
agent_relevance: The closest tested engineering analogue of a distinctive, discriminating key. Add a distinguishing context line to each stored memory.
